    Math 11 — Elementary Statistics

    §2.3

    Other Displays of Data

    The right picture for the data you have

    §2.3 Objectives

    MATH 11

    Today’s Goal

    • Create and interpret dotplots and stem-and-leaf plots
    • Distinguish between appropriate uses of bar graphs and histograms
    • Identify and interpret pie charts and Pareto charts
    • Use Excel to create line graphs, bar graphs, and pie charts
    • Recognize deceptive graphical displays and their misleading features

    §2.3 Learning Target

    MATH 11

    What You Will Be Graded On

    LT.5 Graphical Summaries of Data

    I understand the different types of graphical displays for data (e.g., bar graphs, histograms, boxplots, etc.). I can interpret and create appropriate graphical summaries for various types of data.

    §2.3 Think About It

    MATH 11

    Twenty Numbers, What Picture?

    Twenty adults had their resting heart rate measured, in beats per minute.

    • 72
    • 64
    • 86
    • 66
    • 58
    • 70
    • 63
    • 75
    • 66
    • 81
    • 61
    • 78
    • 64
    • 55
    • 69
    • 72
    • 66
    • 74
    • 71
    • 68

    What picture would you draw?

    A histogram is one answer. Today you get nine more, and the real skill is choosing.

    §2.3 Dotplots

    MATH 11

    Every Value Gets a Dot

    Definition 2.3.1

    A dotplot is a graph of quantitative data in which each data value is plotted as a point (or dot) above a horizontal scale of values. Dots representing equal values are stacked.

    Draw a number line. Put one dot per value. Stack the repeats. That is the whole recipe.

    §2.3 Example 1

    MATH 11

    Reading a Dotplot

    1. (a) Describe the shape.Approximately symmetric, with one peak in the 60s.
    2. (b) How many adults had a heart rate of 66?3, the tallest stack.
    3. (c) What is the most common range?The 60s. Nine of the twenty dots sit there.

    §2.3 Stem-and-Leaf Plots

    MATH 11

    Split Each Value in Two

    Definition 2.3.4

    A stem-and-leaf plot (or stemplot) is a graph of quantitative data in which each data value is separated into two parts:

    • the leaf is the last significant digit in the data value, and
    • the stem is the rest of the data value.

    Each stem appears on its own row with the associated leaves listed to the right of the stem.

    §2.3 Example 2

    MATH 11

    Same Data, New Picture

    The twenty heart rates from Example 1.

    1. (a) What values are in the first row?55 and 58.
    2. (b) Smallest and largest heart rate?55 and 86: first leaf, last leaf.
    3. (c) Turn your head sideways. What do you see?The dotplot’s shape, with every value kept and sorted.
    Stem-and-leaf plot.
    StemLeaves
    55 8
    61 3 4 4 6 6 6 8 9
    70 1 2 2 4 5 8
    81 6

    §2.3 Line Graphs

    MATH 11

    Connect the Dots

    Definition 2.3.7

    A line graph is a visual representation of data that consists of points connected by straight line segments. The horizontal axis typically represents the independent variable such as time or categories, while the vertical axis represents the dependent variable such as quantities or measurements.

    §2.3 Time-Series Graphs

    MATH 11

    Time Along the Bottom

    Definition 2.3.11

    A time-series graph is a graph of time-series data, which are quantitative data that have been collected at different points in time.

    It is a line graph with time on the horizontal axis. It is the graph you see in the news every day.

    §2.3 Example 3

    MATH 11

    Trends Over Time

    A campus café counted its iced coffee sales each month for a year.

    1. (a) Busiest month, and about how many?July, about 590.
    2. (b) The trend from January to July?Up every month, slowly and then fast.
    3. (c) About how many in October?About 330, read off the gridlines.

    §2.3 Bar Graphs

    MATH 11

    Bars for Categories

    Definition 2.3.17

    A bar graph is a graph of bars of equal width to show frequencies (or relative frequencies) of categories for categorical (or qualitative) data. The bars may or may not be separated by small gaps.

    Categorical data. That one word is the whole difference from a histogram.

    §2.3 Think About It

    MATH 11

    Bar Graph or Histogram?

    Both are bars. Both show frequencies. Students mix them up all the time.

    What decides which one you draw?

    Three differences between a bar graph and a histogram.
    Bar graphHistogram
    DataCategorical (qualitative)Quantitative
    BarsMay have gapsTouch, unless the data has a gap
    OrderAny order you likeFollows the number line

    §2.3 Example 4

    MATH 11

    How Did You Get to Campus Today?

    Sixty students in a statistics class answered. Bars are in alphabetical order.

    1. (a) Which way was most common?By car: 27 of the 60.
    2. (b) How many came by bus?12.
    3. (c) Why not a histogram?“Bike” and “Car” are categories, not numbers.

    §2.3 Pareto Charts

    MATH 11

    Tallest First

    Definition 2.3.21

    A Pareto chart is a bar graph in which the categories are arranged in descending order of frequency so the bars decrease in height from left to right.

    Same bars as a bar graph. Only the order changes, and the biggest category jumps out.

    §2.3 Example 4, continued

    MATH 11

    The Same Sixty Students, Reordered

    Example 4 again, tallest bar first.

    1. (a) The campus wants fewer car trips. Where to start?Car. Nothing else comes close.
    2. (b) Which two categories make up the majority?Car and Bus: 27 + 12 = 39 of 60, or 65%.

    §2.3 Pie Charts

    MATH 11

    Slices of One Whole

    Definition 2.3.24

    A pie chart is a graph that depicts categorical data as slices of a circle, in which the size of each slice is proportional to the frequency count for the category.

    Good for parts of one whole. Weak when two slices are close in size.

    §2.3 Example 4, continued

    MATH 11

    The Same Sixty Students, as a Pie

    Example 4 a third time. Percents are rounded to whole numbers.

    1. (a) Which category is the largest slice?Car, just under half the circle.
    2. (b) About what percent came by car?45%, which is 27 out of 60.
    3. (c) Why is Bike versus Walk hard to compare?Nearly equal slices. The bar graph shows 9 versus 8.

    §2.3 Practice

    MATH 11

    Now You Try: Read the Pie

    You Try 2.3.2.

    250 students said where they ate lunch yesterday.

    1. (a) Most common answer?Food court, 36%.
    2. (b) How many ate food from home?0.14 × 250 = 35 students.
    3. (c) Percent not food court or off campus?100 − 36 − 20 = 44%.

    §2.3 Pictographs

    MATH 11

    Pictures That Count

    Definition 2.3.28

    A pictograph is a type of data visualization that uses symbols or pictures to represent data. In a pictograph, each symbol or picture typically represents a certain quantity or value of the data being presented.

    Always find the key first. One symbol is rarely one thing.

    §2.3 Example 5

    MATH 11

    Library Books by Club

    The pictograph shows how many library books each of five student clubs checked out this month.

    1. (a) How many did Robotics check out?5½ symbols × 4 = 22 books.
    2. (b) Which club checked out the fewest?Debate: 1½ symbols, so 6 books.
    3. (c) How many more books did Art check out than Hiking?16 − 8 = 8 more books.

    §2.3 Deceptive Displays

    MATH 11

    When the Axis Lies

    Definition 2.3.38

    A graph has a nonzero axis when one or both of its axes do not begin at 0. Sometimes this is appropriate (for example, to avoid large blank regions in the graph), but a nonzero axis can also be used to misrepresent data by visually exaggerating differences between values.

    Not always a trick. The question is whether the missing zero changes what you see.

    §2.3 Deceptive Displays

    MATH 11

    6.0 Million Against 7.1 Million

    §2.3 Deceptive Displays

    MATH 11

    Pictures That Grow Two Ways

    Adult smoking fell from 37% in 1970 to 18% in 2013. That is about half.

    Does the small cigarette look like half of the big one?

    No. It looks like a quarter. The small picture is half as long and half as wide. Half of a half is a quarter of the area.

    §2.3 Deceptive Displays

    MATH 11

    Bars That Ignore Their Own Numbers

    A TV station asked viewers how concerned they were about the Zika virus.

    What is wrong with this graph?

    The bars do not match the numbers. 13% gets the tallest bar and 34% the shortest. Read the numbers, not the bars.

    §2.3 Deceptive Displays

    MATH 11

    A Pie That Adds Up to 193%

    A TV poll of Republican voters before the 2012 presidential primaries.

    What is wrong with this pie chart?

    70% + 63% + 60% = 193%. A pie is one whole, so its slices must add to 100%. Voters could back more than one candidate, so this is not pie chart data at all.

    §2.3 Deceptive Displays

    MATH 11

    Which Categories, and Since When?

    A faculty union graph of how CSU spending has changed since 2019.

    The scale is honest. What is the problem?

    What counts as “Management Costs”? The categories are never defined, so nobody can check what is in each bar.

    And why 2019? The starting year is a choice. A different start year can tell a different story.

    §2.3 Deceptive Displays

    MATH 11

    Five Tricks to Watch For

    1. Nonzero axis. Starting the vertical axis above zero exaggerates differences.
    2. Inconsistent scales. Two graphs meant to be compared, drawn on different scales.
    3. 3D effects. Depth and perspective make heights and slices hard to compare.
    4. Pictograph scaling. Growing a picture in both height and width distorts the ratio.
    5. Omitting data. Showing only the years, or the categories, that make the point.

    Sometimes it is an accident. Sometimes it is not. Either way, your job is to notice.

    §2.3 Scatter Plots

    MATH 11

    Two Numbers From Each Person

    Definition 2.3.33

    Paired data (also called bivariate data) consists of two quantitative values collected from the same individual or object. Each pair of values (x,y) represents:

    • The explanatory variable (or independent variable) x: the variable that may explain or predict the other
    • The response variable (or dependent variable) y: the variable that may be affected or predicted

    §2.3 Scatter Plots

    MATH 11

    One Point Per Person

    Definition 2.3.34

    A scatter plot (or scatterplot) is a graph that displays paired data as points on a coordinate plane. Each point represents one individual:

    • The x-coordinate corresponds to the explanatory variable
    • The y-coordinate corresponds to the response variable

    Scatter plots reveal patterns, trends, and the form of the relationship between two variables.

    §2.3 Example 6

    MATH 11

    Practice Minutes and Free Throws

    Paired data for eight players: practice minutes per day and free throws made out of 20.
    Practice (minutes a day)510152025303540
    Free throws made (of 20)89121315141718
    1. (a) Which variable is explanatory?Practice. It may explain the score, so it is x.
    2. (b) What pattern do the points show?They rise together. Players who practice more tend to make more free throws. Chapter 12 measures how strongly.

    §2.3 Practice

    MATH 11

    Now You Try: Pick the Picture

    You Try 2.3.3.

    Match each data set to its best display.

    Stem-and-leaf, histogram, time-series, bar graph, pie chart, scatter plot. One is never used.

    Five data sets and the display that fits each.
    The data, and what you want to showDisplay
    Ages of 15 book club members, every age keptStem-and-leaf plot
    A school budget split among departmentsPie chart
    Park visitors, counted monthly for three yearsTime-series graph
    Birth weights of 500 newborns, in classesHistogram
    Favorite pizza topping of 80 studentsBar graph
